claim: Telacebec (Q203) is one of only a few new classes of compounds in more than 50 years with demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans.
source: The imidazopyridine telacebec, also known as Q203, is one of only a few new classes of compounds in more than 50 years with demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical trial data (de Jager et al., 2020) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Telacebec inhibits the mycobacterial respiratory supercomplex composed of complexes III and IV (CIII2CIV2).
source: Telacebec inhibits the mycobacterial respiratory supercomplex composed of complexes III and IV (CIII2CIV2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including activity assays and structural analysis.

claim: In mycobacterial electron transport chains, CIII2CIV2 replaces canonical CIII and CIV.
source: In mycobacterial electron transport chains, CIII2CIV2 replaces canonical CIII and CIV, transferring electrons from the intermediate carrier menaquinol to the final acceptor, molecular oxygen, while simultaneously transferring protons across the inner membrane to power ATP synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claim: CIII2CIV2 transfers electrons from menaquinol to molecular oxygen while simultaneously transferring protons across the inner membrane to power ATP synthesis.
source: In mycobacterial electron transport chains, CIII2CIV2 replaces canonical CIII and CIV, transferring electrons from the intermediate carrier menaquinol to the final acceptor, molecular oxygen, while simultaneously transferring protons across the inner membrane to power ATP synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of CIII2CIV2.

claim: Telacebec inhibits the menaquinol:oxygen oxidoreductase activity of purified Mycobacterium smegmatis CIII2CIV2 at concentrations similar to those needed to inhibit electron transfer in mycobacterial membranes and Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in culture.
source: We show that telacebec inhibits the menaquinol:oxygen oxidoreductase activity of purified Mycobacterium smegmatis CIII2CIV2 at concentrations similar to those needed to inhibit electron transfer in mycobacterial membranes and Mycobacterium tuberculosis growth in culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Telacebec prevents menaquinol oxidation by blocking two different menaquinol binding modes to prevent CIII2CIV2 activity.
source: The structures suggest that telacebec prevents menaquinol oxidation by blocking two different menaquinol binding modes to prevent CIII2CIV2 activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural data obtained by cryoEM.

claim: Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death by infectious disease internationally in most years.
source: In most years, TB is the leading cause of death by infectious disease internationally, with an increasing incidence of drug-resistant infections (Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020.

claim: There is an increasing incidence of drug-resistant tuberculosis infections.
source: In most years, TB is the leading cause of death by infectious disease internationally, with an increasing incidence of drug-resistant infections (Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020.

claim: Mycobacterium leprae causes leprosy.
source: Nontuberculosis mycobacterial pathogens include Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy, Mycobacterium ulcerans, which causes Buruli ulcer, and Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium abscessus, which infect immunocompromised and cystic fibrosis patients, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial pathogens.

claim: Mycobacterium ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer.
source: Nontuberculosis mycobacterial pathogens include Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy, Mycobacterium ulcerans, which causes Buruli ulcer, and Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium abscessus, which infect immunocompromised and cystic fibrosis patients, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial pathogens.

claim: Mycobacterium avium infects immunocompromised patients.
source: Nontuberculosis mycobacterial pathogens include Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy, Mycobacterium ulcerans, which causes Buruli ulcer, and Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium abscessus, which infect immunocompromised and cystic fibrosis patients, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial pathogens.

claim: Mycobacterium abscessus infects cystic fibrosis patients.
source: Nontuberculosis mycobacterial pathogens include Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy, Mycobacterium ulcerans, which causes Buruli ulcer, and Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium abscessus, which infect immunocompromised and cystic fibrosis patients, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial pathogens.

claim: Bedaquiline was discovered from a phenotypic screen with non-pathogenic Mycobacterium smegmatis.
source: The discovery of bedaquiline from a phenotypic screen with non-pathogenic Mycobacterium smegmatis, and its subsequent development into an effective therapeutic, has revolutionized the treatment of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant TB (Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020; World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020 and World Health Organization, 2019.

claim: Bedaquiline has revolutionized the treatment of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant TB.
source: The discovery of bedaquiline from a phenotypic screen with non-pathogenic Mycobacterium smegmatis, and its subsequent development into an effective therapeutic, has revolutionized the treatment of multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant TB (Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020; World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the Global Tuberculosis Report, 2020 and World Health Organization, 2019.

claim: Bedaquiline binds the membrane region of mycobacterial ATP synthase.
source: Bedaquiline binds the membrane region of mycobacterial ATP synthase (Andries et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2021; Preiss et al., 2015), blocking proton translocation and ATP synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andries et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2021; Preiss et al., 2015.

claim: Bedaquiline blocks proton translocation and ATP synthesis.
source: Bedaquiline binds the membrane region of mycobacterial ATP synthase (Andries et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2021; Preiss et al., 2015), blocking proton translocation and ATP synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Andries et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2021; Preiss et al., 2015.

claim: Bedaquiline established oxidative phosphorylation as a target space for antibiotics against mycobacteria.
source: Thus, in addition to providing an invaluable therapeutic tool, bedaquiline established oxidative phosphorylation as a target space for antibiotics against mycobacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the success of bedaquiline as a therapeutic.

claim: Numerous compounds have been identified that target either ATP synthase or the electron transport chain complexes that establish the transmembrane proton motive force.
source: Subsequent to the discovery of bedaquiline, numerous compounds have been identified that target either ATP synthase or the electron transport chain complexes that establish the transmembrane proton motive force (PMF) that drives ATP synthesis (Cook et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claim: In mammalian mitochondrial electron transport chains, complexes I and II oxidize NADH and succinate, respectively.
source: In mammalian mitochondrial electron transport chains, complexes I and II oxidize NADH (the reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and succinate, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claim: Electrons from NADH and succinate are used to reduce a membrane-bound pool of ubiquinone to ubiquinol in mammalian mitochondria.
source: The electrons from these substrates are used to reduce a membrane-bound pool of ubiquinone (UQ) to ubiquinol (UQH2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claim: Electrons from ubiquinol are passed successively to CIII, soluble cyt. c, and CIV before ultimately reducing molecular oxygen to water in mammalian mitochondria.
source: Electrons from UQH2 are then passed successively to CIII (also known as cytochrome [cyt.] bc1), soluble cyt. c, and CIV (also known as cyt. c oxidase or cyt. aa3) before ultimately reducing molecular oxygen to water.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claim: Complexes I, III, and IV couple electron transfer to proton transfer across the membrane in mammalian mitochondria.
source: Complexes I, III, and IV couple electron transfer to proton transfer across the membrane, thereby generating the PMF that drives ATP synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian electron transport chains.

claim: Mycobacteria possess a branched electron transport chain.
source: In contrast to mitochondria and many bacteria, mycobacteria possess a branched electron transport chain (reviewed in Cook et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claim: Mycobacterial respiration relies on menaquinone as an intermediate electron carrier rather than ubiquinone.
source: Rather than UQ, mycobacterial respiration relies on menaquinone (MQ) as an intermediate electron carrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial electron transport chains, supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claim: MQH2 can reduce molecular oxygen via two MQH2:O2 oxidoreductases in mycobacteria: cyt. bd and cyt. bcc-aa3.
source: MQH2 can reduce molecular oxygen via two MQH2:O2 oxidoreductases: cyt. bd and cyt. bcc-aa3, the latter being equivalent to a combination of canonical CIII and CIV with the stoichiometry CIII2CIV2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claim: CIII2CIV2 transfers three protons across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2.
source: The CIII2CIV2 supercomplex and cyt. bd branches of the mycobacterial electron transport chain are bioenergetically not equivalent, while CIII2CIV2 transfers three protons across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2, cyt. bd transfers the equivalent of only one proton across the membrane for each electron.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the bioenergetics of mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claim: Cyt. bd transfers the equivalent of only one proton across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2.
source: The CIII2CIV2 supercomplex and cyt. bd branches of the mycobacterial electron transport chain are bioenergetically not equivalent, while CIII2CIV2 transfers three protons across the membrane for each electron used to reduce O2, cyt. bd transfers the equivalent of only one proton across the membrane for each electron.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the bioenergetics of mycobacterial electron transport chains.

claim: Enzyme utilization in mycobacterial electron transport chains can adapt to changes in environmental conditions and treatment with respiratory complex inhibitors.
source: Enzyme utilization in mycobacterial electron transport chains can adapt to changes in environmental conditions and treatment with respiratory complex inhibitors (Arora et al., 2014; Berney and Cook, 2010), which complicates targeting of respiration by antimycobacterial drugs (Beites et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arora et al., 2014; Berney and Cook, 2010; Beites et al., 2019.

claim: A dimeric type C superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an integral component of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex from M. smegmatis.
source: Structural analysis of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex from M. smegmatis led to the discovery that a dimeric type C superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an integral component of the assembly (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: The SOD dimer is found on the periplasmic side of CIII2CIV2.
source: The SOD dimer is found on the periplasmic side of CIII2CIV2 and is held in place by its two N-terminal tails, which bind to the complex's QcrA subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: The SOD dimer is held in place by its two N-terminal tails, which bind to the complex's QcrA subunits.
source: The SOD dimer is found on the periplasmic side of CIII2CIV2 and is held in place by its two N-terminal tails, which bind to the complex's QcrA subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: QcrA has 81.4% sequence similarity and 73.2% sequence identity between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis.
source: Both QcrA and the SOD subunits are highly conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis, with 81.4% and 71.0% sequence similarity and 73.2% and 64.8% sequence identity, respectively, suggesting that a similar association occurs in the M. tuberculosis enzyme.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: SOD subunits have 71.0% sequence similarity and 64.8% sequence identity between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis.
source: Both QcrA and the SOD subunits are highly conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis, with 81.4% and 71.0% sequence similarity and 73.2% and 64.8% sequence identity, respectively, suggesting that a similar association occurs in the M. tuberculosis enzyme.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: A similar SOD association likely occurs in the M. tuberculosis CIII2CIV2 enzyme.
source: Both QcrA and the SOD subunits are highly conserved between M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis, with 81.4% and 71.0% sequence similarity and 73.2% and 64.8% sequence identity, respectively, suggesting that a similar association occurs in the M. tuberculosis enzyme.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation data.

claim: M. tuberculosis mutants that lack SOD are susceptible to killing within macrophages.
source: M. tuberculosis mutants that lack SOD are susceptible to killing within macrophages (Piddington et al., 2001), emphasizing the importance of the subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piddington et al., 2001.

claim: The SOD subunit may abstract electrons from reactive oxygen species formed during respiration or generated by host-defense mechanisms and direct them through the respiratory chain to contribute to the PMF and ATP synthesis.
source: Given its position within CIII2CIV2, it is possible that the SOD subunit abstracts electrons from reactive oxygen species formed during respiration or generated by host-defense mechanisms in the phagolysosome upon phagocytosis of M. tuberculosis and directs them through the respiratory chain to contribute to the PMF and ATP synthesis (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the position of SOD within CIII2CIV2.

claim: Killing of M. tuberculosis with electron transport chain inhibitors may require simultaneously blocking both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd branches for oxygen reduction.
source: Although killing of M. tuberculosis with electron transport chain inhibitors may require simultaneously blocking both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd branches for oxygen reduction (Arora et al., 2014; Beites et al., 2019; Matsoso et al., 2005), high-profile candidate TB therapeutics have been identified that bind to CIII within CIII2CIV2 (Pethe et al., 2013; Rybniker et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arora et al., 2014; Beites et al., 2019; Matsoso et al., 2005.

claim: High-profile candidate TB therapeutics have been identified that bind to CIII within CIII2CIV2.
source: Although killing of M. tuberculosis with electron transport chain inhibitors may require simultaneously blocking both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd branches for oxygen reduction (Arora et al., 2014; Beites et al., 2019; Matsoso et al., 2005), high-profile candidate TB therapeutics have been identified that bind to CIII within CIII2CIV2 (Pethe et al., 2013; Rybniker et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pethe et al., 2013; Rybniker et al., 2015.

claim: CIII2CIV2 is not essential in M. smegmatis.
source: Similarly, while CIII2CIV2 is not essential in M. smegmatis, its disruption causes severe growth defects (Matsoso et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsoso et al., 2005.

claim: Disruption of CIII2CIV2 causes severe growth defects in M. smegmatis.
source: Similarly, while CIII2CIV2 is not essential in M. smegmatis, its disruption causes severe growth defects (Matsoso et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matsoso et al., 2005.

claim: CIII2CIV2 is essential in M. leprae and M. ulcerans.
source: In contrast, CIII2CIV2 is essential in M. leprae and M. ulcerans, which lack the cyt. bd branch of the electron transport chain entirely (Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009.

claim: M. leprae and M. ulcerans lack the cyt. bd branch of the electron transport chain entirely.
source: In contrast, CIII2CIV2 is essential in M. leprae and M. ulcerans, which lack the cyt. bd branch of the electron transport chain entirely (Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2001; Demangel et al., 2009.

claim: CIII contributes to the PMF by separating positive and negative charges across the membrane through a mechanism known as the Q cycle.
source: Rather than pumping protons, CIII contributes to the PMF by separating positive and negative charges across the membrane through a mechanism known as the Q cycle (reviewed in Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015; Xia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CIII function, supported by citations to Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015; Xia et al., 2013.

claim: Each CIII contains two sites where redox reactions with MQ occur: a QP site near the positive side of the membrane and a QN site near the negative side of the membrane.
source: Each CIII contains two sites where redox reactions with MQ occur: a QP site near the positive (periplasmic) side of the membrane where MQH2 is oxidized and a QN site near the negative (cytoplasmic) side of the membrane where MQ is reduced.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CIII structure and function.

claim: Oxidation of MQH2 in the QP site leads to release of two protons to the positive side of the membrane.
source: In the current understanding of the Q cycle in mycobacteria, oxidation of MQH2 in the QP site leads to release of two protons to the positive side of the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claim: The first electron from MQH2 oxidation is passed to a [2Fe–2S] Rieske center in subunit QcrA where it consecutively reduces the cyt. cc domain of the QcrC subunit and the CuA di-nuclear center of CIV.
source: The first electron from this oxidation reaction is passed to a [2Fe–2S] Rieske center (FeS) in subunit QcrA where it consecutively reduces the cyt. cc domain of the QcrC subunit and the CuA di-nuclear center of CIV.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claim: The second electron from MQH2 in the QP site is transferred first to heme bL and then heme bH before reducing a MQ molecule in the QN site to MQ•-.
source: The second electron from the MQH2 in the QP site is transferred first to heme bL and then heme bH, both in subunit QcrB of CIII, before reducing a MQ molecule in the QN site to MQ•-.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claim: Within CIV, electrons are transferred from the CuA di-nuclear center to O2 bound at the heme a3-CuB binuclear catalytic site via heme a, driving proton pumping across the membrane.
source: Within CIV, electrons are transferred from the CuA di-nuclear center to O2 bound at the heme a3-CuB binuclear catalytic site via heme a, driving proton pumping across the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CIV function.

claim: Telacebec was identified in a screen of macrophages infected with M. tuberculosis.
source: Telacebec (also known as Q203) was identified in a screen of macrophages infected with M. tuberculosis (Pethe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pethe et al., 2013.

claim: Generation of resistance mutants bearing T313I and T313A mutations in the qcrB gene indicated that telacebec targets CIII of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex.
source: Generation of resistance mutants bearing T313I and T313A mutations in the qcrB gene indicated that telacebec targets CIII of the CIII2CIV2 supercomplex.
evidence: This is an inference based on resistance mutation data, supported by citation to Pethe et al., 2013.

claim: A recent Phase 2 clinical trial demonstrated a decrease in viable mycobacterial sputum load with increasing dose of telacebec.
source: A recent Phase 2 clinical trial demonstrated a decrease in viable mycobacterial sputum load with increasing dose of telacebec, supporting further development and making telacebec one of only a few new drug classes in more than 50 years with demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans (de Jager et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Jager et al., 2020.

claim: Telacebec may have clinical utility in treating nontuberculosis mycobacterial infections, such as Buruli ulcer.
source: Telacebec may also have clinical utility in treating nontuberculosis mycobacterial infections, such as Buruli ulcer (Almeida et al., 2020; Van Der Werf et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2020; Van Der Werf et al., 2020.

claim: The M. tuberculosis telacebec resistance mutations T313A and T313I are equivalent to mutation of Thr308 in M. smegmatis.
source: The M. tuberculosis telacebec resistance mutations T313A and T313I (Pethe et al., 2013), equivalent to mutation of Thr308 in M. smegmatis, are near the QP site and suggest that the inhibitor could interfere with MQH2 binding to CIII2CIV2.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: The telacebec resistance mutations are near the QP site and suggest that the inhibitor could interfere with MQH2 binding to CIII2CIV2.
source: The M. tuberculosis telacebec resistance mutations T313A and T313I (Pethe et al., 2013), equivalent to mutation of Thr308 in M. smegmatis, are near the QP site and suggest that the inhibitor could interfere with MQH2 binding to CIII2CIV2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of resistance mutations and structural data.

claim: Purification of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis grown in TDS-supplemented medium gave a high yield of enzyme with clear bands on an SDS-PAGE gel for most of the known subunits of the complex.
source: Purification of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis grown in these conditions gave a high yield of enzyme with clear bands on an SDS-PAGE gelfor most of the known subunits of the complex (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Gel filtration chromatography of CIII2CIV2 led to depletion of the LpqE and SOD subunits.
source: We observed that following affinity purification, gel filtration chromatography of the enzyme led to depletion of the LpqE and SOD subunits (Figure 1A, right) compared to affinity purification alone (Figure 1A, left), and consequently this purification step was avoided.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CryoEM of the CIII2CIV2 preparation allowed for calculation of a 3D map of the enzyme at a nominal resolution of 3.0 Å.
source: CryoEM of the CIII2CIV2 preparation allowed for calculation of a 3D map of the enzyme at a nominal resolution of 3.0 Å (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Table 1.

claim: The cryoEM map shows strong density for the LpqE subunit.
source: The map shows strong density for the LpqE subunit (Figure 1B, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: LpqE was observed in one previous structural study of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis but was absent in another.
source: LpqE was observed in one previous structural study of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis (Gong et al., 2018) but was absent in another (Wiseman et al., 2018), presumably due to depletion of the subunit during purification of the supercomplex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018 and Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: In the structure missing LpqE, the cyt. cc domain of subunit QcrC adopts both an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation.
source: In the structure missing LpqE, the cyt. cc domain of subunit QcrC adopts both an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation, while the structure with LpqE was found only in the closed conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: The structure with LpqE was found only in the closed conformation of the cyt. cc domain.
source: In the structure missing LpqE, the cyt. cc domain of subunit QcrC adopts both an 'open' and a 'closed' conformation, while the structure with LpqE was found only in the closed conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claim: The closed conformation creates a direct electronic connection between heme cII of CIII and CuA of CIV.
source: The closed conformation creates a direct electronic connection between heme cII of CIII and CuA of CIV (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: In the open conformation, heme cII from the cyt. cc domain is too far from CuA to allow electron transfer.
source: In the open conformation, heme cII from the cyt. cc domain is too far from CuA to allow electron transfer, leading to the hypothesis that switching between the closed and open conformations plays a role in controlling the flow of electrons through the supercomplex (Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: Switching between the closed and open conformations of the cyt. cc domain may play a role in controlling the flow of electrons through the supercomplex.
source: In the open conformation, heme cII from the cyt. cc domain is too far from CuA to allow electron transfer, leading to the hypothesis that switching between the closed and open conformations plays a role in controlling the flow of electrons through the supercomplex (Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations, supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: LpqE was hypothesized to strengthen the physical attachment between CIII and CIV.
source: In contrast, LpqE was hypothesized to strengthen the physical attachment between CIII and CIV (Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claim: 3DVA revealed complexes with and without LpqE.
source: 3DVA with the current dataset (Punjani and Fleet, 2021), focused on one half of the supercomplex, revealed complexes with and without LpqE.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 3DVA analysis.

claim: Where LpqE was missing, the cyt. cc domain exhibits the open conformation.
source: Where LpqE was missing, the cyt. cc domain exhibits the open conformation, while complexes with LpqE show only the closed conformation of cyt. cc (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claim: Complexes with LpqE show only the closed conformation of cyt. cc.
source: Where LpqE was missing, the cyt. cc domain exhibits the open conformation, while complexes with LpqE show only the closed conformation of cyt. cc (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claim: Clashes between LpqE and the open conformation of cyt. cc suggest that LpqE prevents the open conformation.
source: Clashes between LpqE and the open conformation of cyt. cc suggest that LpqE prevents the open conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The SOD subunit of CIII2CIV2 was poorly resolved in previous cryoEM maps and appeared as a diffuse density.
source: In previous studies, the SOD subunit of CIII2CIV2 was poorly resolved in cryoEM maps and appeared as a diffuse density (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: In the present map, the overall shape of SOD was more readily apparent than in previous studies.
source: In the present map, the overall shape of SOD, although still at lower density than the rest of the complex, was more readily apparent (Figure 1B, pink).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The N-terminal anchors from the SOD dimer that bind to subunit QcrB are well resolved and terminate at the middle of the complex with a lipid anchor.
source: The N-terminal anchors from the SOD dimer that bind to subunit QcrB are well resolved and terminate at the middle of the complex with a lipid anchor (Figure 1B, beige).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 3DVA shows that SOD moves between the center of the complex to immediately above heme cI.
source: 3DVA (Figure 1C, Video 2) shows that SOD moves between the center of the complex, where it was observed previously (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018) to immediately above heme cI.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claim: The proximity of SOD to heme cI suggests that SOD may transfer electrons abstracted from superoxide in the periplasm to CIV to contribute to the PMF.
source: This proximity suggests that SOD may indeed transfer electrons abstracted from superoxide in the periplasm of M. smegmatis to CIV to contribute to the PMF (Gong et al., 2018; Wiseman et al., 2018), although this hypothesis requires further testing.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on structural observations.

claim: The overall resolution of the map allowed refinement of an atomic model for CIII2CIV2 including residues that could not be modeled previously.
source: The overall resolution of the map, which is somewhat better than in previous studies, allowed refinement of an atomic model for CIII2CIV2 including residues T82, E83, A123 to D131, and S183 from LpqE, and residues H57 to G78 from MSMEG_4693 (also known as CtaJ), which could not be modeled previously (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Table 1.

claim: The mycobacterial electron transport chain uses MQH2 as the electron donor for CIII2CIV2.
source: The mycobacterial electron transport chain uses MQH2 as the electron donor for CIII2CIV2 while in canonical mitochondrial electron transport chains UQH2 donates electrons to CIII2 (Cook et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claim: In canonical mitochondrial electron transport chains UQH2 donates electrons to CIII2.
source: The mycobacterial electron transport chain uses MQH2 as the electron donor for CIII2CIV2 while in canonical mitochondrial electron transport chains UQH2 donates electrons to CIII2 (Cook et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Cook et al., 2017.

claim: The midpoint potentials of the redox centers in mycobacterial CIII2 are lower than those of canonical mitochondrial CIII2.
source: The midpoint potentials of the redox centers in mycobacterial CIII2 are lower than those of canonical mitochondrial CIII2 (Kao et al., 2016), and as a result UQH2 analogues typically used in CIII2 assays are not able to reduce CIII2 of the M. smegmatis supercomplex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kao et al., 2016.

claim: UQH2 analogues typically used in CIII2 assays are not able to reduce CIII2 of the M. smegmatis supercomplex.
source: The midpoint potentials of the redox centers in mycobacterial CIII2 are lower than those of canonical mitochondrial CIII2 (Kao et al., 2016), and as a result UQH2 analogues typically used in CIII2 assays are not able to reduce CIII2 of the M. smegmatis supercomplex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference in midpoint potentials.

claim: MQH2 analogues capable of reducing CIII2CIV2 suffer from autoxidation at neutral or basic pH.
source: MQH2 analogues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) capable of reducing CIII2CIV2 suffer from autoxidation at neutral or basic pH, which leads to oxygen reduction even in the absence of enzyme (Munday, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claim: Autoxidation of MQH2 analogues leads to oxygen reduction even in the absence of enzyme.
source: MQH2 analogues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) capable of reducing CIII2CIV2 suffer from autoxidation at neutral or basic pH, which leads to oxygen reduction even in the absence of enzyme (Munday, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claim: The rate of autoxidation was proposed to be ~30% slower for DMWH2 compared to menadiol at pH 7.5.
source: Although both substrates are susceptible to autoxidation, the rate of autoxidation was proposed to be ~30% slower for DMWH2 compared to menadiol at the pH 7.5 of our oxygen consumption assays (Munday, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claim: Menaquinol autoxidized more slowly than DMWH2.
source: In contrast to these earlier studies, we found that menaquinol autoxidized more slowly than DMWH2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Menadiol was substantially less efficient than DMWH2 as an electron donor for CIII2CIV2.
source: However, we also found that mendiol was substantially less efficient than DMWH2 as an electron donor for CIII2CIV2, likely due to its less favorable redox potential (Fieser and Fieser, 1934), supporting the choice of DMWH2 as the substrate in assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citation to Fieser and Fieser, 1934.

claim: At low concentrations of CIII2CIV2 the SOD subunit suppresses autoxidation of DMWH2 more than CIII2CIV2 catalyzes oxidation of DMWH2.
source: On subsequent investigation, we realized that at low concentrations of CIII2CIV2 the SOD subunit suppresses autoxidation of DMWH2 more than CIII2CIV2 catalyzes oxidation of DMWH2.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Suppression of quinol autoxidation by SOD has been described previously.
source: This suppression of quinol autoxidation by SOD, which has been described previously (Cadenas et al., 1988), can lead to apparent negative activities for CIII2CIV2 when the background autoxidation is subtracted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cadenas et al., 1988.

claim: Autoxidation of quinols is believed to involve a superoxide anion intermediate.
source: Autoxidation of quinols is believed to involve a superoxide anion intermediate, with the SOD-catalyzed dismutation of the intermediate to hydrogen peroxide removing this reactant to slow the process (Munday, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Munday, 2000.

claim: Bovine C-type SOD can limit the autoxidation of DMWH2.
source: To remove error introduced by the effect of the SOD subunit on the observed oxygen reduction signal, we established that bovine C-type SOD can similarly limit the autoxidation of DMWH2 (Figure 2A, blue and orange curves), as well as menadiol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: With 500 nM SOD added, the CIII2CIV2's DMWH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity was measured at 91 ± 4 e-/s.
source: With 500 nM SOD added, the CIII2CIV2's DMWH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity was measured at 91 ± 4 e-/s (± s.d., n = 6 independent assays with three each from two separate batches of protein), which is nearly an order of magnitude greater than the apparent activity found previously (Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from activity assays.

claim: The measured CIII2CIV2 activity is nearly an order of magnitude greater than the apparent activity found previously.
source: With 500 nM SOD added, the CIII2CIV2's DMWH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity was measured at 91 ± 4 e-/s (± s.d., n = 6 independent assays with three each from two separate batches of protein), which is nearly an order of magnitude greater than the apparent activity found previously (Wiseman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous data supported by citation to Wiseman et al., 2018.

claim: Titrations of CIII2CIV2 activity with varying concentrations of telacebec show an IC50 of 53 ±19 nM with 65 nM CIII2CIV2 and 100 µM DMWH2.
source: Titrations of CIII2CIV2 activity with varying concentrations of telacebec (Figure 2C) show an IC50 of 53 ±19 nM (± s.d., n = 3 independent titrations, with two titrations from one batch of purified protein and a third titration from a second batch of purified protein) with 65 nM CIII2CIV2 and 100 µM DMWH2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The IC50 of telacebec for purified CIII2CIV2 is lower than the 840 ± 22 nM seen with the menadiol-based assay.
source: This IC50 is lower than the 840 ± 22 nM seen with the menadiol-based assay (Gong et al., 2018), but higher than the 20 nM concentration needed to inhibit 50% of respiratory chain activity with inverted membrane vesicles from M. smegmatis (Lu et al., 2018) or 2.7 nM required to inhibit the 50% of M. tuberculosis growth in liquid culture (Pethe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous data supported by citations to Gong et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2018; Pethe et al., 2013.

claim: The IC50 of telacebec for purified CIII2CIV2 is higher than the 20 nM concentration needed to inhibit 50% of respiratory chain activity with inverted membrane vesicles from M. smegmatis.
source: This IC50 is lower than the 840 ± 22 nM seen with the menadiol-based assay (Gong et al., 2018), but higher than the 20 nM concentration needed to inhibit 50% of respiratory chain activity with inverted membrane vesicles from M. smegmatis (Lu et al., 2018) or 2.7 nM required to inhibit the 50% of M. tuberculosis growth in liquid culture (Pethe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous data supported by citation to Lu et al., 2018.

claim: The IC50 of telacebec for purified CIII2CIV2 is higher than the 2.7 nM required to inhibit 50% of M. tuberculosis growth in liquid culture.
source: This IC50 is lower than the 840 ± 22 nM seen with the menadiol-based assay (Gong et al., 2018), but higher than the 20 nM concentration needed to inhibit 50% of respiratory chain activity with inverted membrane vesicles from M. smegmatis (Lu et al., 2018) or 2.7 nM required to inhibit the 50% of M. tuberculosis growth in liquid culture (Pethe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous data supported by citation to Pethe et al., 2013.

claim: The increased IC50 in the current assay compared to assays with inverted membrane vesicles or bacterial growth may be due to the binding affinity or high concentration of DMWH2.
source: The increased IC50 in the current assay compared to assays with inverted membrane vesicles or bacterial growth in liquid culture may be due to the binding affinity or high concentration of DMWH2, which could allow DMWH2 to compete with telacebec for binding to the complex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences in IC50 values.

claim: Differences in inhibition in the different assays could be due to CIII2CIV2 being in detergent micelles rather than a lipid bilayer.
source: In addition, differences in inhibition in the different assays could be due to CIII2CIV2 being in detergent micelles rather than a lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences in IC50 values.

claim: The QP site is near the periplasmic side of the membrane, located between heme bL and the FeS cluster.
source: The QP site is near the periplasmic side of the membrane, located between heme bL and the FeS cluster (Figure 3A), and is formed by several loops and α helices from both the QcrB and QcrA subunits (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CIII structure, supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The arrangement of structural elements in the QP site is conserved from other CIIIs.
source: The arrangement of structural elements in the site is conserved from other CIIIs (Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015.

claim: In the inhibitor-free structure there is density for endogenous MQ in the QP site.
source: In the inhibitor-free structure there is density for endogenous MQ in the QP site (Figure 3B, pale blue surface).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The head group of MQ matches the density at 4.4σ.
source: With the standard deviation of the cryoEM map normalized to σ = 1, the head group of MQ matches the density at 4.4σ.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of the density in the cryoEM map.

claim: The symmetry of the MQ head group makes it difficult to determine which of two poses, related by a 180° rotation, is correct.
source: However, even with this strong density, the symmetry of the head group (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) makes it difficult to determine which of two poses, related by a 180° rotation, is correct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis of the cryoEM map.

claim: The naphthoquinone head group of MQ is positioned near the entrance to the QP site, between the F and C helices.
source: The naphthoquinone head group of MQ is positioned near the entrance to the site, between the F and C helices (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: This position for endogenous MQ was reported in a previous study of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis.
source: This position for endogenous MQ was reported in a previous study of CIII2CIV2 from M. smegmatis (Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claim: In the observed position, the naphthoquinone head group is ~14 Å away from the FeS cluster.
source: In this position, the naphthoquinone head group is ~14 Å away from the FeS cluster and the hydroxyl proton is ~15 Å from His368, which is too far for rapid coupled electron and proton transfer from MQH2 to FeS and His368, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural model.

claim: The hydroxyl proton of MQ is ~15 Å from His368 in the observed position.
source: In this position, the naphthoquinone head group is ~14 Å away from the FeS cluster and the hydroxyl proton is ~15 Å from His368, which is too far for rapid coupled electron and proton transfer from MQH2 to FeS and His368, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural model.

claim: The observed distance is too far for rapid coupled electron and proton transfer from MQH2 to FeS and His368.
source: In this position, the naphthoquinone head group is ~14 Å away from the FeS cluster and the hydroxyl proton is ~15 Å from His368, which is too far for rapid coupled electron and proton transfer from MQH2 to FeS and His368, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about electron transfer distances.

claim: The position of endogenous MQ contrasts the deeper binding position adopted by UQ in ovine CIII2.
source: This distance contrasts the deeper binding position adopted by UQ in ovine CIII2 (Letts et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous structural data supported by citation to Letts et al., 2019.

claim: The position of endogenous MQ is further from the FeS than the position observed for UQ-analogue inhibitors bound to chicken or bovine CIII2.
source: It is also further from the FeS than the position observed for UQ-analogue inhibitors such as stigmatellin bound to chicken CIII2 (Zhang et al., 1998), as well as 5-undecyl-6-hydroxy-4,7-dioxobenzothiazole (Esser et al., 2004) and 2-n-nonyl-4-hydroxyquinoline N-oxide (Gao et al., 2003) bound to bovine CIII2.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous structural data supported by citations to Zhang et al., 1998; Esser et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2003.

claim: In the deeper position the head groups of UQ or its analogues are wedged between the ef helix/loop, and the cd1 helix.
source: In the deeper position the head groups of UQ or its analogues are wedged between the ef helix/loop, and the cd1 helix, with the tail trailing between the F and C helix at the QP site entrance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of structural features observed in previous studies, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The distance between the quinone head group and the FeS cluster can be as little as ~7 Å in structures with UQ or its analogues.
source: In these structures, the distance between the quinone head group and the FeS cluster depends on the position of the mobile Rieske head domain, but can be as little as ~7 Å, allowing for rapid electron transfer from the UQH2 to the FeS (Moser et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moser et al., 2006.

claim: Initial attempts to image CIII2CIV2 with telacebec failed to resolve the inhibitor.
source: Our initial attempts to image CIII2CIV2 with telacebec failed to resolve the inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, left), leading us to consider the possibility that inhibitor binding occurs during substrate turnover by the enzyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CryoEM of CIII2CIV2 in the presence of DMWH2 but without telacebec confirmed that the density in the QP site was indistinguishable from MQ seen with the enzyme at rest.
source: CryoEM of CIII2CIV2 in the presence of DMWH2 but without telacebec confirmed that under these conditions the density in the QP site was indistinguishable from MQ seen with the enzyme at rest (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The structure of CIII2CIV2 with both DMWH2 and telacebec was determined to a nominal resolution of 3.0 Å by cryoEM.
source: We then incubated CIII2CIV2 with both DMWH2 and telacebec to produce an inhibited complex and determined the structure of this complex to a nominal resolution of 3.0 Å by cryoEM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: Telacebec binding did not cause large-scale conformational changes in CIII2CIV2.
source: Telacebec binding did not cause large-scale conformational changes in CIII2CIV2 but produced a clear density for the inhibitor in each of the two QP sites in the CIII2 dimer (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Telacebec produced a clear density in each of the two QP sites in the CIII2 dimer.
source: Telacebec binding did not cause large-scale conformational changes in CIII2CIV2 but produced a clear density for the inhibitor in each of the two QP sites in the CIII2 dimer (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The inhibitor's imidazopyridine moiety, amide linker region, and A-phenyl and B-piperidinyl moieties are all resolved clearly in the structure.
source: The inhibitor's imidazopyridine moiety, amide linker region, and A-phenyl and B-piperidinyl moieties are all resolved clearly, with weaker density toward the end of the tail, which points into the lipid bilayer toward the cytoplasmic side of the membrane (Figure 3C, pale blue surface).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Telacebec binds with its head group deep within the QP binding pocket in a pose similar to UQ and the UQ-analogue inhibitors bound within the canonical CIII2.
source: These densities show that telacebec binds with its head group deep within the QP binding pocket in a pose similar to UQ and the UQ-analogue inhibitors bound within the canonical CIII2 as described above (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous structures shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The position of the N1 nitrogen in telacebec's imidazopyridine moiety is consistent with formation of a hydrogen bond with His368 from the QcrA subunit.
source: Although hydrogen bonds cannot be detected with complete confidence at the present resolution, the position of the N1 nitrogen in telacebec's imidazopyridine moiety is consistent with formation of a hydrogen bond with the His368 from the QcrA subunit, which also binds the FeS group (Figure 3C and D, dashed teal line).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: A similar hydrogen bond between UQ and the equivalent histidine residue in canonical CIII2 has been proposed to coordinate the Q cycle.
source: The occurrence of a similar hydrogen bond between UQ and the equivalent histidine residue in canonical CIII2 (Zhang et al., 1998) has been proposed to coordinate the Q cycle (e.g. see Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 1998 and Sarewicz and Osyczka, 2015.

claim: The 2-ethyl group from the imidazopyridine is ~4 Å away from Ile178 from the QcrB subunit, providing hydrophobic interactions.
source: The 2-ethyl group from the imidazopyridine is ~4 Å away from Ile178 from the QcrB subunit, providing hydrophobic interactions (Figure 3C and D, dashed green line), while the 6-chloro group from the imidazopyridine is close to the backbone carboxyl group of Leu166 from the QcrB subunit, enabling formation of a possible halogen bond (Figure 3C and D, dashed purple line).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural model shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The 6-chloro group from the imidazopyridine is close to the backbone carboxyl group of Leu166 from the QcrB subunit, enabling formation of a possible halogen bond.
source: The 2-ethyl group from the imidazopyridine is ~4 Å away from Ile178 from the QcrB subunit, providing hydrophobic interactions (Figure 3C and D, dashed green line), while the 6-chloro group from the imidazopyridine is close to the backbone carboxyl group of Leu166 from the QcrB subunit, enabling formation of a possible halogen bond (Figure 3C and D, dashed purple line).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Thr308 is <4 Å away from the linker region of telacebec.
source: Thr308, which is homologous with M. tuberculosis Thr313 and is known to be important for binding (Pethe et al., 2013), is <4 Å away from the linker region of telacebec.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural model.

claim: One of the rotamer states of Thr308 could form a stabilizing hydrogen bond with the carbonyl group of the linker region of telacebec.
source: Although the rotameric state of Thr308 is ambiguous at the current resolution, one of the rotamer states could form a stabilizing hydrogen bond with the carbonyl group of the linker region (Figure 3C and D, dashed teal line).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Phe156 is ~3.5 Å from the A-phenyl group of telacebec, allowing for aromatic-aromatic interaction.
source: Finally, Phe156 is ~3.5 Å from the A-phenyl group of telacebec, allowing for aromatic-aromatic interaction between the protein and inhibitor (Burley and a, 1985; Figure 3C and D, dashed pink line)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural model shown in Figure 3C and D, supported by citation to Burley and a, 1985.

claim: In the inhibitor-free specimen, the MQ head group is positioned similarly to the A-phenyl ring of telacebec and may form similar stabilizing contacts with the QcrB subunit.
source: Interestingly, in the inhibitor-free specimen, the MQ head group is positioned similarly to the A-phenyl ring of telacebec and may form similar stabilizing contacts with the QcrB subunit (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the two structures shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The structural analysis provides constraints and minimal requirements for activity of imidazopyridines and isosteric heterocycles with improved pharmacokinetic and physicochemical properties.
source: However, the structural analysis reported here provides constraints and minimal requirements for activity of imidazopyridines and isosteric heterocycles with improved pharmacokinetic and physicochemical properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data presented.

claim: Optimized physicochemical properties are important for drug production, including synthesis and purification.
source: Optimized physicochemical properties are important for drug production, including synthesis and purification.
evidence: This is established knowledge about drug development.

claim: Improved pharmacokinetic properties could be enabled by design of analogues that retain target activity but are not recognized by mycobacterial efflux pumps.
source: Improved pharmacokinetic properties could be enabled by design of analogues that retain target activity but are not recognized by mycobacterial efflux pumps, which are known to remove telacebec from bacterial cells to attenuate its antimycobacterial activity (Jang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about drug design, supported by citation to Jang et al., 2017.

claim: Mycobacterial efflux pumps are known to remove telacebec from bacterial cells to attenuate its antimycobacterial activity.
source: Improved pharmacokinetic properties could be enabled by design of analogues that retain target activity but are not recognized by mycobacterial efflux pumps, which are known to remove telacebec from bacterial cells to attenuate its antimycobacterial activity (Jang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jang et al., 2017.

claim: The mutation T313A in M. tuberculosis (T308A in M. smegmatis) confers resistance to telacebec.
source: The mutation T313A in M. tuberculosis (T308A in M. smegmatis) confers resistance to telacebec (Pethe et al., 2013), likely by removing the stabilizing hydrogen bond with the carbonyl group from the linker region of the inhibitor proposed above (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pethe et al., 2013.

claim: The T313A mutation likely confers resistance by removing the stabilizing hydrogen bond with the carbonyl group from the linker region of telacebec.
source: The mutation T313A in M. tuberculosis (T308A in M. smegmatis) confers resistance to telacebec (Pethe et al., 2013), likely by removing the stabilizing hydrogen bond with the carbonyl group from the linker region of the inhibitor proposed above (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: M. smegmatis grown in the presence of the telacebec analogue TB47 developed the mutation H190Y.
source: M. smegmatis grown in the presence of the telacebec analogue TB47 developed the mutation H190Y (Lu et al., 2019), which is adjacent to the cd1 helix and may alter the shape of the QP binding site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2019.

claim: The H190Y mutation is adjacent to the cd1 helix and may alter the shape of the QP binding site.
source: M. smegmatis grown in the presence of the telacebec analogue TB47 developed the mutation H190Y (Lu et al., 2019), which is adjacent to the cd1 helix and may alter the shape of the QP binding site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The selectivity of telacebec for mycobacterial CIII2CIV2 may derive, in part, from the lack of Thr308 in mammalian mitochondrial CIII2.
source: The selectivity of telacebec for mycobacterial CIII2CIV2 may derive, in part, from the lack of Thr308 in mammalian mitochondrial CIII2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There may be clashes between the rigid telacebec tail and both Leu150 and Ile146 in mammalian CIII2 due to the different location of the cd1 helix and the bulkier side chains in this region.
source: In addition, there may be clashes between the rigid telacebec tail and both Leu150 and Ile146 in mammalian CIII2 (bovine numbering) due to the different location of the cd1 helix and the bulkier side chains in this region of the mammalian protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mutation I147F (M. smegmatis numbering) results in resistance to the inhibitor stigmatellin in the Saccharomyces cerevisiae CIII2.
source: Interestingly, the mutation I147F (M. smegmatis numbering) results in resistance to the inhibitor stigmatellin in the Saccharomyces cerevisiae CIII2 (di Rago et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to di Rago et al., 1989.

claim: Multiple MQ binding sites were modeled in an earlier 3.5 Å resolution cryoEM density map of CIII2CIV2.
source: Multiple MQ binding sites were modeled in an earlier 3.5 Å resolution cryoEM density map of CIII2CIV2, but the significance of these sites was not clear (Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claim: Telacebec binds only at the QP site.
source: The structure presented here shows that telacebec, which can inhibit MQH2:O2 oxidoreductase activity completely (Figure 2C), binds only at the QP site.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and the structural analysis.

claim: It is unlikely that MQ binding other than within the QP site is involved in electron transfer to oxygen.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that MQ binding other than within the QP site is involved in electron transfer to oxygen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that telacebec binds only at the QP site and completely inhibits activity.

claim: During the Q cycle, two molecules of MQH2 are oxidized to MQ at the QP site for each molecule of MQ reduced to MQH2 at the QN site.
source: During the Q cycle, two molecules of MQH2 are oxidized to MQ at the QP site for each molecule of MQ reduced to MQH2 at the QN site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Q cycle mechanism.

claim: MQ may be channeled between the QP and QN sites by staying loosely bound to the supercomplex surface, with additional MQ sites serving as intermediate positions along the channeling pathway.
source: It is possible that MQ is channeled between the QP and QN sites by staying loosely bound to the supercomplex surface, with the additional MQ sites serving as intermediate positions along the channeling pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about MQ channeling.

claim: A similar channeling model was suggested for the spinach b6f complex.
source: A similar model was suggested for the spinach b6f complex, which is structurally and functionally related to CIII and carries out a Q cycle in plant chloroplasts with the hydrophobic electron carrier plastiquinone (Malone et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Malone et al., 2019.

claim: Alternative MQ sites may sequester MQ, increasing the local concentration of substrate near its two binding sites.
source: It is also possible that these alternative MQ sites sequester MQ, increasing the local concentration of substrate near its two binding sites, which has been seen to increase the local concentration of ligands in other systems (Vauquelin and Charlton, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citation to Vauquelin and Charlton, 2010.

claim: Different positions for both UQ and MQ within the QP site have been described previously for canonical CIII and for CIII within a CIII2CIV2 supercomplex.
source: Within the QP site different positions for both UQ and MQ have been described previously, both for canonical CIII and for CIII within a CIII2CIV2 supercomplex, respectively (Ding et al., 1992; Moe et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ding et al., 1992; Moe et al., 2021.

claim: The endogenous MQ found in the structure is most likely oxidized.
source: Although the endogenous MQ found in the structure is most likely oxidized, the position it occupies is along the access path to the FeS center.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental conditions.

claim: Reduced MQH2 also adopts the Q1b position, at least transiently, during turnover.
source: We speculate that reduced MQH2 also adopts the same position, at least transiently, during turnover.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: Movement of MQH2 deeper within the QP site to a Q1a position would bring it less than 10 Å from FeS, close enough to donate electrons to the redox center and protons to His368.
source: In contrast, movement of MQH2 deeper within the QP site to a Q1a position would bring it less than 10 Å from FeS, close enough to donate electrons to the redox center and protons to His368 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In an emerging model for CIII2CIV2 function, the Q1b position serves as a 'stand-by' site for MQH2, with oxidation of the substrate occurring only upon relocation to Q1a.
source: In an emerging model for CIII2CIV2 function, the Q1b position serves as a 'stand-by' site for MQH2, with oxidation of the substrate occurring only upon relocation to Q1a (see Moe et al., 2021; Mulkidjanian, 2005).
evidence: This is a model based on structural analysis, supported by citations to Moe et al., 2021; Mulkidjanian, 2005.

claim: Telacebec serves as dual site inhibitor, with the imidazopyridine group bound to the Q1a position and A-phenyl portion of the tail bound to the Q1b position.
source: The structure of CIII2CIV2 with telacebec bound shows that the compound serves as dual site inhibitor (Figure 4D), with the imidazopyridine group bound to the Q1a position and A-phenyl portion of the tail bound to the Q1b position.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The possible hydrogen bond between Thr308 and the carboxyl group in the linker region of telacebec could also occur between Thr308 and MQ, stabilizing it in the Q1b position.
source: Indeed, the possible hydrogen bond between Thr308 and the carboxyl group in the linker region of telacebec could also occur between Thr308 and MQ, stabilizing it in the Q1b position.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The observed pose of telacebec not only blocks MQ access to the FeS center but fills the QP site entirely.
source: Therefore, the observed pose of the inhibitor within the enzyme not only blocks MQ access to the FeS center but fills the QP site entirely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Inhibiting CIII2CIV2 has demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans.
source: Inhibiting CIII2CIV2 has demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans (de Jager et al., 2020), even though M. tuberculosis possesses cyt. bd as an alternative enzyme that can oxidize MQH2 and sustain the electron flux to oxygen in the mycobacterial membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Jager et al., 2020.

claim: M. tuberculosis possesses cyt. bd as an alternative enzyme that can oxidize MQH2 and sustain the electron flux to oxygen in the mycobacterial membrane.
source: Inhibiting CIII2CIV2 has demonstrated antituberculosis activity in humans (de Jager et al., 2020), even though M. tuberculosis possesses cyt. bd as an alternative enzyme that can oxidize MQH2 and sustain the electron flux to oxygen in the mycobacterial membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mycobacterial electron transport chain.

claim: More potent killing of mycobacterial pathogens can be accomplished by simultaneous inhibition of both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd terminal oxidases.
source: More potent killing of mycobacterial pathogens can be accomplished by simultaneous inhibition of both the CIII2CIV2 and cyt. bd terminal oxidases (Beites et al., 2019; Kalia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beites et al., 2019; Kalia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2021.
